proof_attempt_summary: D0 developed a refined crossed-cell upper bound and a matched parametric subregion using the accepted parent's converse. D0.5 found that the required full residual-wedge rate, degree-indexed covariance family, and exactly normalized radius-sensitive lower experiment remained open. The corrected theorem wording left two proof statuses stale; no F-stage formalization began. A future attempt needs new proofs of the interior upper and lower branches.
tldr: Sparse discrete adjustment leaves many cells without treated-control crossings, while approximate effect homogeneity permits pooling. The accepted parent fixes the present model's all-alphabet boundary rates: \(\rho_0(n,d)=n^{-1}+\min\{1,d/n^2\}\) at exact homogeneity, \(\rho_2(n,d)=n^{-1}+\min\{1,u\}\) at unrestricted heterogeneity, and \(n^{-1}\) for one cell. These results are inherited. The project seeks an explicit matched minimax MSE frontier only in the shrinking-radius residual wedge, with one total known-radius estimator and a same-class all-estimator converse. Its crossed-cell refinement closes a strict interior subregion; the degree-indexed covariance and exactly normalized prior routes remain candidates. No full interior phase formula is asserted.
gap: Zeng, Balakrishnan, Han, and Kennedy explicitly leave sharp dependence on the maximal heterogeneity radius unresolved. The accepted parent gives only \(b+\sigma^2u\lesssim R/M^2\lesssim b+\min\{u,\sigma^2\}\) in the residual wedge, and its upper and lower proof devices fail for different radius-sensitive reasons.
fill: A finite phase envelope lists the crossed-cell, homogeneous, unrestricted, and degree-indexed marked-factorial upper candidates. Each degree branch has the displayed covariance penalty \(V_K\) and the normalized-prior target \(\Delta_K\), while the saturated branch has target \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sat}}\). The refined crossed-cell theorem supplies a low-degree branch and proves that the old selector cannot be uniformly sharp; the final result retains only branches with matching same-class upper and lower bounds.
